_meta.comment: Hand-authored tips that override the converter's auto-generated tips. Keyed by question id (d1_001, d1_002, ...). Each value is an array of 2-4 short tips. Re-running scripts/convert_test_bank.py merges these into data/domain1.json.

d1_001: Two-sided trap: A says 'IT will pre-audit' — but IT's continuous monitoring is a control activity, not auditing. D says 'auditor can never audit those systems' — but writing detection scripts isn't the same as designing the control framework.

CAATs scripts that flag exceptions are a tool, not a control framework. Sharing them doesn't compromise the auditor's ability to test the underlying transactions, business processes, and other controls.
When IS resources are shared with operations, ask: 'Does the auditor still have independent ways to test what isn't covered by the shared tool?' If yes, sharing is acceptable.
d1_002: A and D feel reasonable (more complex org → more data; familiar org → less data) but neither DRIVES data collection. They are factors that may inform the audit AFTER scope is set.
Purpose, objective, and scope are the audit's north star — every downstream decision (sample size, evidence type, time budget) flows from them.
When you see 'BEST factor for determining the EXTENT' of audit work, look for the option that defines the audit's boundary, not its difficulty or backstory.
d1_003: Trap is A: management is the auditee. Letting them set scope without an independent risk assessment compromises auditor independence — even if their suggestion turns out to be correct.
Management may SUGGEST areas of concern; the auditor must independently VALIDATE through risk assessment. Choice C does both — the assessment may well confirm new systems are highest risk.
Default response when management requests specific scope: thank them, then run a risk assessment. ISACA Standard 1202 makes this mandatory in planning.
d1_004: Audit risk is the umbrella concept: audit risk = inherent × control × detection. The phrase 'during IS auditing' signals the umbrella term, not one of its components.
If the question says 'during the audit / undetected', think audit risk. 'Before any controls' → inherent. 'Controls fail' → control. 'Audit procedures fail' → detection.
ISACA conflates audit risk with material misstatement risk — they're treating the broad 'will I miss something material?' question.
d1_005: Trap is A 'overlapping': sounds related but means TWO controls covering the same objective. That presupposes you have a primary control — in a SoD failure, the primary control is what's missing.
Compensating controls answer: 'We can't implement the ideal control — what else reduces this risk?' Small-team SoD failures almost always demand compensating controls.
Common compensating controls for SoD gaps: enhanced logging + supervisory review, periodic transaction sampling, independent reconciliation, mandatory vacations, job rotation.
d1_006: Trap is C 'fraud detection': it's a real benefit of CSA but a side-effect, not the primary purpose. Don't confuse outcomes with objectives.
CSA's core mechanism is shifting CONTROL OWNERSHIP from audit to business management — making line managers responsible for the controls they live with daily. That's why A wins.
ISACA explicitly distinguishes CSA from internal audit — CSA enhances audit work, it doesn't replace it (immediately rules out D as a 'shift to consultative').
d1_007: Trap is D 'customizable': sounds like the most flexible choice and tools sales pitch favorite. But the PRIMARY requirement is data accuracy without performance impact — customization is nice-to-have.
Auditing tools are 'guests' in production — if the tool degrades the system being audited, the audit itself becomes a business risk and may invalidate the data being captured.
CAATs evaluation order: 1) accuracy of capture → 2) performance impact → 3) compatibility → 4) flexibility/customization.
d1_008: Trap is C 'IT knowledge': feels right (“they know our systems!”). That's exactly the conflict — they have existing relationships and may have worked on the very systems they'd now audit.
Independence is the foundational requirement of any audit role — it overrides all other competencies. Technical knowledge can be acquired; lost independence cannot be restored mid-engagement.
When hiring auditors from operational areas, the screening question is always: 'Which systems and projects did you work on, and which fall under audit scope today?'
d1_009: Trap is A 'CAATs': closely related and effective, but CAATs is a TOOL category. Continuous auditing USES CAATs but adds the real-time + automated reporting layer — the difference matters for 'emerging' risk.
'Emerging' implies time-sensitive: quarterly assessments (B) are too infrequent, log sampling (C) has lag, ad-hoc CAATs (A) still requires you to RUN them on a schedule.
CISA pattern: high transaction volume + emerging risk → continuous auditing. Almost never sampling alone.
d1_010: Two-step distinction: are we testing whether a CONTROL operates correctly (compliance) or whether DATA is accurate (substantive)? 'Were accounts authorized?' is a question about a control — compliance.
Mnemonic: authorization, approval, segregation → compliance. Balances, totals, monetary values → substantive.
A and D are sampling METHODS, not test categories — they self-eliminate when the question asks 'which type of testing is this?'
d1_011: Trap is C 'control': auditors recommend controls but don't implement them. Detection risk is the only risk auditors directly shape — through their choice of procedures, sample size, and expertise.
Risk ownership map: inherent (business nature) → control (management) → detection (auditor) → business (executive/strategy).
Phrase giveaway: 'selection of audit procedures' or 'audit techniques' = detection risk every time.
d1_012: Trap is A 'review prior findings': feels rigorous and IS part of planning, but it's an INPUT to risk assessment, not a substitute. Prior findings tell you about old issues, not current risk landscape.
Risk assessment is the foundation that determines scope, resources, sampling, and procedures. Without it, you're auditing by intuition and exposing the function to coverage gaps.
ISACA Standard 1202 makes risk assessment in planning MANDATORY — not best practice, mandatory. That alone elevates D over the alternatives.
d1_013: Trap is D 'audit core service and dependencies': feels like the right place to dig in, but you can't audit a system you don't yet understand. SOA is a distributed black-box architecture — you must map first, test second.
Canonical sequence for any unfamiliar architecture: documentation review → mapping (services to processes) → controls assessment → transaction testing.
When the question asks for the INITIAL step on a complex system, the answer is almost always 'understand it' — never 'start testing it.'
d1_014: Trap is A 'delete all copies': auditors don't perform remediation. This violates independence (auditor performing operational tasks) and oversteps authority.
Auditor's job: identify → document → report risk to management → recommend prevention. Management decides on remediation, not the auditor.
Anytime an option has the auditor DOING something operational (deleting, blocking, installing, configuring, fixing), it is almost certainly wrong.
d1_015: Trap is B 'state audit objectives': engagement-specific objectives live in the engagement letter, not the charter. The charter is organizational, not project-specific.
The charter is an authority document — it answers 'who, what scope, what authority' for the audit FUNCTION as a whole. Not for individual audits.
Charter content priority: authority > scope > responsibility > reporting line. Procedures (C) and dynamic technology content (A) belong in audit methodology documents, not the charter.
d1_016: Two traps: B 'report to audit committee' jumps past diagnosis; D 'recommend the owner fix it' violates independence before scope is even understood.
Auditors investigate before they recommend: scope the issue (how many, which managers, what type of access) before escalating or proposing fixes.
CISA pattern: 'small number found' + 'something off' = perform additional analysis FIRST. Almost never 'report' or 'recommend fix' as the first step.
d1_017: Attribute sampling = compliance ('does the control exist / fire?'). Variable/stratified/difference = substantive ('how much, how often, by what amount').
Whenever the question is whether a control was applied (a yes/no question), the sampling method is attribute sampling. Always.
d1_018: Trap is D 'create additional sample data' — fabricating audit evidence is a major ethics violation. Auditors test what's there, not what they wish was there.
Trap is B 'report the finding' — premature; lack of available changes isn't itself a finding without further work. Adapt the test approach instead.
When the original test approach can't deliver assurance, change the approach (with audit management approval). Document why and what alternative was used.
d1_019: Trap is D 'consulting on good practices' — discussing principles doesn't impair independence; designing or building specific application controls does.
Trap is C 'project team member without operational responsibilities' — observation/attendance without operational role is allowed, just disclose.
The line is at HANDS-ON BUILD. Discuss principles → fine. Sit in meetings → fine. Implement, code, configure → independence impaired.
d1_020: Continuous audit's value isn't reduced effort — it's reduced LAG between event and audit response. Real-time monitoring → real-time correction.
Continuous audit shifts the audit cycle from periodic snapshots to ongoing surveillance, making issues actionable while still relevant to the business.
Continuous audit doesn't displace responsibility for control monitoring (rules out C); that always stays with management/security.
d1_021: Trap is A 'ensuring compliance with development methods' — that's QA's job. Doing QA's job doesn't impair QA. Correcting code DOES (now QA approves their own corrections).
QA's role is to inspect and report — not to fix. Same independence principle as audit.
Anytime someone validates AND corrects the same artifact, you have a separation-of-duties failure.
d1_022: The other three (skill sets, test steps, time allotted) are downstream of risk identification. You can't allocate skills/time/tests until you know WHERE risk lives.
Risk-based audit planning is the audit profession's central operating principle — every other planning decision is in service of it.
ISACA Standard 1202 mandates risk identification as the foundation of audit planning, not an optional good practice.
d1_023: Trap is A 'control design testing' — design testing answers 'is the control conceived correctly?', not 'is it operating effectively?'. Operational effectiveness needs substantive evidence.
Trap is C 'documentation inspection' — documents may say one thing, the actual operation another. Documentation review by itself is weak evidence.
Substantive testing examines the actual transactions and records produced — the most direct evidence of whether the control is doing its job.
d1_024: Same answer pattern as the planning-extent question (d1_002): data collection extent is set by audit purpose and scope, never by auditor familiarity, auditee evidence ability, or data availability.
If evidence is hard to find, the auditor finds an alternative method, not a smaller sample. Difficulty doesn't shrink scope.
Recurring CISA pattern: 'extent of audit work' ALWAYS ties back to audit scope/purpose, never to the convenience or familiarity of the people involved.
d1_025: Trap is B 'definite assurance' — definite/absolute is impossible in audit; CISA always uses 'reasonable'.
Trap is C/D 'all items' — covering all items isn't realistic or even desirable; the goal is coverage of MATERIAL items.
Audit always works with reasonable assurance + materiality. Anytime you see 'definite', 'absolute', or 'all items' in an option, eliminate it immediately.
d1_026: Trap is D 'request the IDs be removed' — auditor doesn't get to request operational changes. They report; management decides.
Trap is A 'inform audit committee' — premature; document and report through normal channels first.
Auditor lifecycle: identify → document → report risk → recommend → defer remediation to management. Steps 4+ skip ahead, step 1 (D) is operational interference.
d1_027: Compliance tests answer 'does the control work as intended?'. They don't measure efficiency (A) — that's a management metric, not an audit one.
Trap is C 'integrity of data controls' — that's substantive testing's territory. Compliance is about CONTROL operation, substantive is about DATA accuracy.
Mnemonic: Compliance → Conformance to design. Substantive → Substance/data accuracy.
d1_028: Trap is C 'integrated test facility' — ITF tests current processing as it happens, not historical retroactive analysis. The question asks about LAST YEAR's data.
Trap is D 'embedded audit module' — same issue: forward-looking, not retroactive.
Generalized audit software is the right tool for retroactive analysis of large historical datasets — it can recompute, stratify, and identify duplicates without modifying production.
d1_029: Trap is A 'create the procedures' — auditor writing the documentation is a textbook independence violation.
Trap is B 'end the audit' — lack of documentation is a finding, not a stop signal. The audit's purpose is to identify risk; absence of documentation IS risk to surface.
Auditors test what exists, including informal/undocumented practices. Then report the documentation gap as a finding so management can address it.
d1_030: The risk analysis loop: identify assets → identify threats + impacts → evaluate existing controls → assess residual risk → recommend additional controls. The question places you between threat identification and risk calculation.
Trap is C 'disclose to management' — premature; disclosure happens after the analysis is complete, not mid-flow.
Risk = (threat × impact) MODERATED by existing controls. You can't quantify residual risk until you know what existing controls already mitigate.
d1_031: Reliability hierarchy: independent third-party > auditor's own work > internal system-generated > management assertion > internet/general data.
Trap is B 'line management assurance' — single weakest evidence type because management has direct interest in the audit outcome.
The key word is 'independent' — the more disconnected the evidence source from the auditee's interest, the more reliable it is.
d1_032: Trap is B 'only preventive and detective relevant' — corrective controls matter too; they reduce damage even when prevention fails.
Trap is C 'corrective = compensating' — different concepts. Compensating substitutes for missing primary controls; corrective fixes problems after detection.
Controls operate at specific points in data flow (input, processing, output). Their collective effectiveness depends on which points are covered and which are gap.
d1_033: Trap is D 'testing user access rights' — system access is necessary but not sufficient. Real SoD failures often happen through workarounds, shared credentials, or informal task delegation that don't show up in access tables.
Trap is B 'org chart' — describes intended structure, not actual practice.
Observation reveals what people ACTUALLY do; interviews reveal what they THINK they do. Together they detect the gap between formal access and actual behavior.
d1_034: Trap is A 'obtain management approval of corrective action' — corrective action plan ownership belongs to management, but approval is not the auditor's role.
Trap is C 'assist management in implementation' — implementation assistance violates auditor independence.
The closing meeting is the auditor's last chance to validate facts before publishing the report. Errors caught here protect both auditor and auditee.
d1_035: Trap is B 'authorizations' — authorization happens at transaction time, not at reconciliation time.

Trap is A 'vouching' — vouching matches recorded transactions to source documents (record → source). Tracing matches source documents to records (source → record). Reconciliation needs the upward direction.
Mnemonic: Tracing follows the journey forward (source → destination). Vouching looks backward (record → original source).
d1_036: Trap is C 'dated screenshot from sysadmin' — admin can modify settings before screenshotting. Trap is A 'admin spreadsheet' — same risk + manual transcription error.
Evidence reliability key: who handled it? If the auditee handled it, it's tampered until proven otherwise.
The auditor should pull configuration data directly whenever possible. Auditor-acquired evidence ≥ third-party evidence > auditee-provided evidence.
d1_037: Trap is B 'authenticity' — checksums detect corruption/tampering but don't prove sender identity. Authenticity needs digital signatures or MACs.
Mnemonic: Checksum = Change detection. Doesn't authenticate, doesn't authorize, just integrity.
Layered EDI controls: integrity (checksum/hash) + authenticity (signature) + authorization (transaction limits) + nonrepudiation (full PKI). Each requires its own mechanism.
d1_038: Tests performed under audit standards beat third-party letters because letters are subject to interpretation and not always conducted under formal audit methodology.
Trap is D 'confirmation letter from outside source' — would be #1 if not for the explicit option of an external auditor's tests. Procedures > assertions.
Subtle CISA pattern: when the choice is between 'auditor-conducted procedure' and 'third-party signed letter', the procedure wins.
d1_039: Trap is A 'EDI trading partner agreements' — agreements are legal protection, not technical prevention. Contracts don't stop unauthorized packets.
Trap is D 'program change control' — applies to system changes, not to runtime transaction authentication.
Unauthorized transactions = authentication failure. When 'unauthorized' is the symptom, look for authentication-strengthening options first.
d1_040: Trap is B 'reports with sign-off' — a signature without follow-up evidence proves only that someone touched the report, not that they reviewed exceptions.
Effective review = look at exceptions + take action. The presence of action items is the operational evidence.
CISA pattern for control effectiveness: a control that 'fires' but has no follow-up is a control that doesn't work — verify the follow-up loop, not just the trigger.
d1_041: Functional acknowledgments are EDI-native — they confirm that the receiving system parsed and accepted the structure. That's the data mapping audit trail.
Trap is A 'key verification' — used in encryption and data entry validation, not in EDI data mapping.
Trap is B 'one-for-one checking' — verifies completeness of transmission, not the correctness of the mapping.
d1_042: Same as d1_017: authorization compliance → attribute sampling. The value of the PO doesn't matter, just whether it followed the matrix rule.
Trap is A or B 'variable/stratified mean per unit' — these examine value distribution. Authorization is binary (yes/no) → attribute.
The matrix gives a rule. Compliance with a rule = attribute sampling. Monetary impact = variable sampling. Almost never confused once you learn the cue.
d1_043: Trap is A 'review source code' — code review can identify potential errors but doesn't confirm what the system actually does in practice.
Trap is B 'recreate program logic' — duplicating logic is risky; the auditor's reimplementation may have its own bugs.

Black-box testing with known inputs and predetermined expected outputs is the cleanest way to verify any calculation — auditor doesn't need to understand HOW it computes, only WHETHER it computes correctly.
d1_044: Application control review's purpose is risk assessment — what can go wrong, and how bad would it be.
Trap is A or D 'efficiency / optimization' — those are operational metrics, not audit objectives.
Trap is C 'business processes served' — that's an audit prerequisite (understanding scope), not the focus of the controls evaluation.
d1_045: Trap is B/C 'do not include because resolved' — the audit report must reflect the period audited, not a snapshot at publication time.
Including the finding + the corrective action protects the auditee (shows responsiveness) AND ensures the issue is documented for future audits.
CISA pattern: the audit report is a permanent record of conditions found during fieldwork. Discoveries don't disappear because they were quickly fixed.
d1_046: Discovery sampling answers: 'has at least one occurrence of [event] happened?' — perfect for fraud screening (you only need to find one to expose a pattern).
Trap is D 'probability-proportional-to-size' — used when financial value matters; fraud screening is about occurrence, not value.
Trap is A 'stop-or-go' — used to limit sample size when expected exception rate is very low; not specifically fraud-tuned.
d1_047: The strategy phase identifies WHAT to focus on (areas, systems, processes). That requires knowing where threats meet vulnerabilities.
Trap is A 'controls in place' — that's an output of the audit, not an input to the strategy.
Risk-based strategy precedes audit; controls testing is what the audit does. Don't confuse the planning input with the audit deliverable.
d1_048: Trap is A 'sign release form' — confrontational and outside auditor authority.
Trap is D 'accept auditee position' — caves on professional judgment; auditee disagreement isn't grounds for retraction.
The auditor's job in disputes is to clarify the risk so the auditee fully understands what's at stake — then management can make an informed decision about acceptance vs. remediation.
d1_049: Trap is A 'schedule and monitor time' — operational, downstream of planning.
Trap is B 'train staff on technology' — staff capability is enabling, not the FIRST step.
Risk-based planning is the only thing that ensures audit resources go to high-value targets. Without it, you're optimizing the wrong thing.
d1_050: Trap is C 'include in report with comments' — premature; the auditor should first verify their own evidence before locking it into the report.
Trap is A 'retest the control' — retesting is downstream of evidence revalidation. If the evidence is sound, retesting may be unnecessary.
CISA disputes 101: when challenged, the auditor first verifies they have it right, then either confirms the finding or revises it. Never both publishes AND verifies in parallel.
